questiontext.text: Which pair of operations does a disjoint-set (union-find) structure primarily support?

answer.text: FIND (representative of an element's set) and UNION (merge two sets)

feedback.text: Correct — FIND returns a set's representative and UNION merges two sets.

answer.text: INSERT and DELETE of a key in sorted order

feedback.text: That describes a search tree, not a disjoint-set structure.

answer.text: PUSH and POP from the top

feedback.text: Those are stack operations.

answer.text: ENQUEUE and DEQUEUE by priority

feedback.text: That describes a priority queue.

generalfeedback.text: Union-find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets, exposing FIND (which set an element belongs to) and UNION (merge two sets).

questiontext.text: With union by rank/size and path compression, what is the amortized time per operation?

answer.text: O(α(n)) — inverse Ackermann, effectively near-constant

feedback.text: Correct — α(n) ≤ 4 for any practical n, so operations are near-constant amortized.

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: That is the bound with only one optimization; combining both gives near-constant.

answer.text: O(n)

feedback.text: Far too slow — the whole point is near-constant amortized cost.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: That is a sorting bound, unrelated to a single union-find operation.

generalfeedback.text: Union by rank/size keeps trees shallow and path compression flattens them, giving O(α(n)) amortized, where α is the inverse Ackermann function (≤ 4 in practice).

questiontext.text: What does path compression do during a FIND operation?

answer.text: It re-points visited nodes directly to the root, flattening the tree

feedback.text: Correct — later FINDs on those nodes become almost immediate.

answer.text: It sorts the elements of the set in ascending order

feedback.text: Disjoint sets are unordered; no sorting happens.

answer.text: It deletes the smaller set to save memory

feedback.text: No elements are deleted; sets are merged, not removed.

answer.text: It rebalances the tree like an AVL rotation

feedback.text: Union-find uses no rotations; it just redirects parent pointers to the root.

generalfeedback.text: Path compression makes every node visited on the way to the root point straight at the root, so subsequent FINDs are nearly O(1).

questiontext.text: Which algorithm most naturally uses a disjoint-set structure?

answer.text: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (detecting whether an edge joins two components)

feedback.text: Correct — union-find tracks components and rejects edges that would form a cycle.

answer.text: Dijkstra's shortest path with a priority queue

feedback.text: Dijkstra relies on a priority queue, not union-find.

answer.text: Binary search on a sorted array

feedback.text: That needs an ordered array, unrelated to disjoint sets.

answer.text: In-order traversal of a BST

feedback.text: Traversal is a tree operation, not a set-partition problem.

generalfeedback.text: Classic uses include connected components, Kruskal's MST, and cycle detection in an undirected graph — all built on FIND/UNION.

questiontext.text: Which statements about disjoint-set structures are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Union by rank/size attaches the shorter/smaller tree under the taller/larger one

feedback.text: Yes — this keeps the trees shallow.

answer.text: It maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets

feedback.text: Yes — every element belongs to exactly one set.

answer.text: It supports efficient range-sum queries over an array

feedback.text: No — that is a Fenwick/segment tree task, not union-find.

answer.text: It is a self-balancing binary search tree

feedback.text: No — it is a forest of up-trees, not a search tree.

generalfeedback.text: Union-find is a partition maintained as up-trees with union by rank/size; it does not do ordered search or range queries.

questiontext.text: A disjoint-set (union-find) structure is a kind of self-balancing binary search tree.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — it is a forest of "up-trees" that only need parent pointers toward a root; there is no key ordering.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — it maintains a set partition, not an ordered search tree.

questiontext.text: Combining path compression with union by rank/size gives near-constant amortized time per operation.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — together they yield O(α(n)) amortized, effectively constant.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: They do combine to give the O(α(n)) amortized bound.

questiontext.text: The near-constant amortized bound of union-find is expressed with the inverse ______ function.

answer.text: Ackermann

feedback.text: Correct — the bound is O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function.

answer.text: Ackermann*

feedback.text: Correct.
